html:
Chanakya, also called Kautilya, was by tradition the Brahmin teacher who put Chandragupta Maurya on the throne of Magadha about 322 BCE and then served as his chief minister. His dates are guesses; later legend is almost the only source.

The story, told in Buddhist, Jain and Hindu versions, runs like this. Chanakya was insulted at the court of the Nanda king at Pataliputra and swore to destroy the dynasty. He found the young Chandragupta, trained him, and together they raised an army in the northwest after Alexander left. Their first attack on the capital failed. Chanakya is said to have learnt from a mother scolding her child for eating from the hot middle of a dish and not from the cool edges. They then took the outer provinces first and the capital last.

He is named as the author of the Arthashastra, the great Sanskrit book on statecraft, though the text as it stands is later.

In India his name stands for a clever and hard political mind. The diplomatic quarter of New Delhi is called Chanakyapuri after him.
